props.text: 1 Consent by Dr/ Somaya Madkour Professor of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology Alexandria University 2 Consent ILO’s. 1. Differentiate types of consents in the medical field. 2. Apply the principals of informed consent and how to be valid and documented. 3. Differentiate the exceptions to require a consent. 4. Respect the patient’s right to refuse treatment. Consent is a central topic in bioethics. It lies at the heart of the relationship between the patient and the health care professional. The patient relies on the professional’s expertise, knowledge and advice, but it is up to the patient to decide whether he/she will accept or reject treatment, or in some circumstances request that the professional make the decision. What does consent mean?? a) Consent is the giving of permission or agreement for an intervention (whether diagnostic or therapeutic) following a process of communication about the proposed intervention. b) Consent must be obtained before starting treatment or investigations, or providing personal or social care for a patient or involving a patient in teaching and research. c) All patients have the right to be involved in decisions about their treatment and care and to make informed decisions if they can. d) The exchange of information between doctor and patient is essential to good decision making. serious harm can result if patients are not listened to, or if they are not given the information they need - and time and support to understand it - so they can make informed decisions about their care. Obtaining valid consent is an ethical obligation and legal compulsion • Informed consent is essential to ethics, which upholds the principles of autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice: • Treating a patient without informed consent could result in legal action for assault against the Health Practitioner who provided the care, irrespective of whether the patient suffered harm as a result of the procedure (constitutes medical malpractice). Consent in medical practice is needed in the following situations: 1-Examination of a patient for the purpose of diagnosis and subsequent treatment. 2- Examination of a patient for medico-legal purposes. 3- Involving patients in medical research studies. Why is consent important? • To protect the patient from unauthorized procedures. • To protect the physician from claims of malpractice. If the consent is not obtained, the patient has the right to sue for medical malpractice Types of consent: 1- Implied consent (Known by the behavior of the patient) • The act of a patient entering a doctor's chamber and expressing his problem is taken as an implied consent for general physical examination (patient has consented to abdominal 3 palpation when voluntarily undressing and lying on couch) and routine investigations such as X-rays etc… • When he/she offers an arm for venipuncture (giving a blood sample). • The act of the patient standing in line to receive a vaccination. • Express (oral or written) consent It means that the Patient expressly asks the doctor to provide care and consents by direct words, oral or written. This consent should be obtained for any procedure that carries any risk, and therefore, patient-specific agreement must be obtained before the procedure starts. • The patient or his/her representative has the right to be provided with sufficient information by the physician to allow him/her to make an informed decision to decide whether or not to consent to a certain procedure. Oral consent is valid, but it is usual to obtain written consent for major procedures. a) Oral consent: ▪ For intimate examinations e.g., vaginal and rectal. ▪ Simple procedures e.g., insertion of an intravenous cannula. ▪ Procedures performed under local anesthesia e.g., suture of minor lacerations. b) Written consent: For more invasive tests or for major procedures with significant risks e.g. ▪ blood transfusion ▪ breast biopsy ▪ all operations requiring general or spinal anesthesia. What are the requirements for obtaining a valid consent? 1) the patient giving consent must have capacity 2) the consent must be freely given 3) the consent must be sufficiently specific to the procedure or treatment proposed 4) the consent must be informed. The four criteria for a valid consent must be met irrespective of whether the consent is in writing or oral. 1) Capacity The patient must have the capacity to give consent. A person has decision making capacity if they can: • understand the facts and choices involved • weigh up the consequences and evaluate the personal cost and benefit of each of the consequences and relate them to your own set of values and priorities • communicate their decision. Legally, adults are presumed to have capacity to consent to or refuse medical treatment unless otherwise indicated. A person is incapable of giving consent to the carrying out of medical treatment if the person: (a) is incapable of understanding the general nature and effect of the proposed treatment, or (b) is incapable of indicating whether or not he or she consents or does not consent to the treatment being carried out General principles to follow when assessing capacity: • always presume a person has capacity 4 • capacity is decision-specific (for example capacity may fluctuate or certain simple health treatments may be within a person’s capacity to consent whilst others may not) • respect a person’s privacy • substitute decision making is a last resort 2) Freely given: Consent must be freely given. The patient must not be pressured, coerced or intimidated into giving consent by Health Service staff, a Health Practitioner, a carer or a family member. 3) Sufficiently specific: The consent must be specific and is valid only for the condition being treated and the specified treatment or procedure about which the patient has been informed and agreed to. 4) Informed: The patient must be informed in broad terms of the nature and purpose in a way that the patient can understand. Health Practitioners have a duty to provide the patient with enough information to enable them to gain an understanding of the nature and effects of the operation, procedure or treatment, the risks associated with it and any alternatives to the proposed treatment. • So consent must be given voluntary by an appropriately informed patient who has the capacity to consent to the proposed procedure (the patient or his guardian as in case of minor responsible about them) • If the patient does not know what the intervention entails …. it is not consent • If patients are not able to do all of the components, family members, court- appointed guardians, or others (as determined by law) may act as "surrogate decision-makers" and make decisions for you. • A valid Consent is not given for illegal act as criminal abortion and euthanasia. Sometimes ethical beliefs and legal rights do not always coincide. We cannot legally consent to voluntary euthanasia, since it is illegal, even if we feel strongly that it should be permitted. • A valid Informed Consent should be obtained by a health care provider who is involved with the patient's care. The seven principles of decision making and consent Every physician should be familiar with this document (GMC guidelines) 1) All patients have the right to be involved in decisions about their treatment and care and be supported to make informed decisions if they are able. 2) Decision making is an ongoing process focused on meaningful dialogue: ( it is not one way thing , it is 2 way and sometimes family member , friends may be involved ) the exchange of relevant information specific to the individual patient. 3) All patients have the right to be listened to, and to be given the information they need to make a decision and the time and support they need to understand it. 4) Doctors must try to find out what matters to patients so they can share relevant information about the benefits and harms of proposed options and reasonable alte

props.text: Values, Beliefs , and Facts Ahmed A Elsheshai MD, MRCPsych psychiatrist Medical procedures for personal values Patients may ask for procedures for their own personal values and beliefs Aesthetic procedures Circumcision Preventive surgery In this case Make sure it is for the best interest of the patient Keep in mind their own religious and social background Take great care with your consent process Children  parents or court Refusal of treatment You must respect a competent patient’s decision to refuse an investigation or treatment, even if you think their decision is wrong or irrational. Children whose parents refuse treatment on religious or cultural background discuss their concerns and look for treatment options that will accommodate their beliefs. Involve the child in a way appropriate to their age and maturity If treatment is life saving and no other option is available, you should approach the court Conscientious objection You may choose to opt out of providing a particular procedure because of your personal beliefs and values, as long as this does not result in direct or indirect discrimination against, or harassment of, individual patients or groups of patients. This means you must not refuse to treat a particular patient or group of patients because of your personal beliefs or views about them. And you must not refuse to treat the health consequences of lifestyle choices to which you object because of your beliefs Discussion of beliefs & Self disclosure You should ask about beliefs and values and try to understand and empathize with the patient wherever possible In doing so you should not ask a patient to justify or discuss these beliefs Example: diabetic patients fasting Ramadan You may talk about your own personal beliefs only if the patient asks or directly indicates that they would welcome such input. In doing so you should only state your beliefs and values without imposition on the patient or causing them distress. Example: stage III cancer patient refuses treatment because they welcome death Example 1 A doctor refuses to perform hepatic transplant to a chronic alcohol user, because: He believes the patient brought this on himself The patient’s blood alcohol level indicates recent intoxication The patient is old and there are younger patients who need this liver The patient’s general condition does not support the major operation Example 2 A doctor treats AIDS but refrains from treating a patient who is promiscuous or homosexual because They increased their chances of contracting the illness by making certain lifestyle choices. They brought this on themselves (divine punishment). According to the ethical construct of justice, treatment and resources should be reserved for people with lower chance of reinfection. According to the doctor’s personal beliefs he chooses to refrain from treating this particular individual. Example 3 A doctor insists that his obese patient must lose weight before he will prescribe any medication, because: He believes the medication will be ineffective (futile) due to morbid obesity The doctor does not believe in intermediary solutions and pain-killers He intends to corner the patient into doing the right thing by denying him pain killers The doctor himself was obese and believes the patient can lose weight as he did Example 4 A plastic surgeon demands psychiatric evaluation to a patient who is requesting rhinoplasty, because: People should not change the way God made them She is from a moderate socio-economic class and there must be better things to spend her money on. He thinks she really looks pretty and that there is no need for any modification He fears that her request may reflect a defect in self-esteem resulting from depression or body dysmorphic disorder Case An 8-week pregnant woman has been exposed to radiation. She was told by her obstetrician that there is a considerable chance that the child has been deformed. There may be grounds for abortion, but the doctor prefers to wait and see if the child really has deformities. The mother is apprehensive and choses to go with abortion anyway because: “why take a risk when I can skip this pregnancy and bear another child”. Outline the values and beliefs of the patient and the doctor. Reflect on the doctor’s choices and what is the best course of action References Sagiv L, Roccas S, Cieciuch J, Schwartz SH. Personal values in human life . Nature Human Behaviour . 2017 Sep;1(9):630 schwarz theory of values Beck JS. Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond. Guilford press; 2011 Jason Giesbrecht. Personal Values and Beliefs Course slides. Plus2019 https://www.gmc-uk.org/-/media/documents/personal-beliefs-and-medical-practice-20200217_pdf-58833376.pdf LOs Differentiate the terms “value” and “belief” Enumerate basic values and identify examples for each List sources of beliefs and identify examples for each Assess their own value and belief systems Correlate the impact of values and beliefs on patient care Solve ethical vignettes related to value and belief conflict. Thank you Value Broad desirable goals that motivate people’s actions and serve as guiding principles in their lives (1) Schwarz theory of basic values (2) Universalism Benevolence Conformity/tradition Security Power Achievement Hedonism Stimulation Self direction Belief Core beliefs are defined as fundamental, inflexible, absolute, and generalised beliefs that people hold about themselves, others, the world, and/or the future (3) Activity Divide into 4 groups. Each group will try to come up with as many values and beliefs about one topic. Smoking Alcohol use Doctors’ immigration Body image Sports Doctors’ personal beliefs Doctors may practice medicine in accordance with their beliefs, provided that they act in accordance with relevant legislation and: do not treat patients unfairly do not deny patients access to appropriate medical treatment or services do not cause patients distress. props.text: 1 Interprofessional & Intraprofessional Relationships in Healthcare By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Define Interprofessional and Intraprofessional Relationships 2. Identify competencies of intra/ interprofessional collaboration 3. Demonstrate effective communication Strategies for collaborating with other healthcare professionals. 4. Discuss Common Barriers to effective professional communication 5. Explain Intra/Interprofessional significance in healthcare settings. 6. Analyze Ethical Issues in Interprofessional Relationships Definitions: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), interprofessional collaboration occurs when “multiple health workers from different professional backgrounds work together with patients, families, caregivers and communities to deliver the highest quality of care across settings.” E.g. collaboration between physicians, nurses, pharmacists, physical therapists and the social care profession. Regarding the intraprofessional relationship, it is the collaboration between two or more disciplines within the same profession e.g. collaboration between a pediatrician and neurosurgeon for the sake of the patient. Competencies of intra/ interprofessional collaboration: Competencies identified for intra/interprofessional collaboration are categorized into six domains: 1. Patient-centered care 2. Interprofessional communication 3. Participatory leadership 4. Conflict resolution 5. Transparency of duties and responsibilities 6. Teamwork 2 1. Patient-centered care: Patient-centered care is one of the main competencies in the healthcare system. It ensures the safety and quality of healthcare. Patient-centered care is the degree to which patients and their families are satisfied with their care and involved in decision making process and to which those providing the care do so with sensitivity and respect for the patient’s need, expectations and individual differences. One of the dimensions of patient-centered care is the coordination and smooth transition from one healthcare setting to another. 2. Intra/ interprofessional communication: It describes the sharing of information (by means of verbal, writing or other medium) among members of different health professionals’ fields in a responsive and responsible manner that supports a team and influence patient care positively. Components of Intra/ Interprofessional Communication • Effective communication tools, information systems and communication technologies that facilitate interactions. • Avoiding discipline-specific terminology when communicating information with patients, families, community members. • Expressing one’s knowledge and opinions to team members with clarity, and respect to ensure common understanding of information. • Active listening to encourage ideas and opinions of other team members. • Giving sensitive, constructive feedback to others about their performance on the team. • Using respectful language in difficult situations, or during conflict. General Barriers to Intra/ Interprofessional Communication: • Personal values and expectations and personality differences • Organizational hierarchy • Varying team members who may not have worked together before • Cultural diversity and generational differences • Historical interprofessional and intraprofessional competitions 3 • Differences in language and medical jargon • Differences in schedules and professional routines • Varying levels of preparation, qualifications, and status • Fears of diluted professional identity • Diverse clinical responsibilities • Increased complexity of patient care • Emphasis on rapid decision-making ISBARR communication model: A common format used by health care team members to exchange client information is ISBARR, a mnemonic for the components of Introduction, Situation, Background, Assessment, Request/Recommendations, and Repeat back. • Introduction: Introduce your name, role, and the agency from which you are calling. • Situation: Provide the patient’s name and location, the reason you are calling, recent vital signs, and the status of the patient. • Background: Provide background information about the patient such as admission date and diagnosis, current condition , recent relevant lab or diagnostic results, previous illnesses and allergies. • Assessment: Share abnormal assessment findings and your evaluation of the current situation. • Request/Recommendations: such as reassessment, order a lab/diagnostic test, prescribe/change medication. • Repeat back: to confirm accuracy. Be sure to document communication in the patient’s chart. 3. Participatory leadership: It is a unique leadership style, also referred to as democratic leadership. Participative leaders recognize the significant role of all members in team success, so they encourage all team members to provide feedback and participate in shared decision-making. They also promote transparent communication and collaborative solutions. 4 4. Conflict resolution: It happens when healthcare providers work as a team that actively engages in addressing disagreements and responding effectively to all types of conflict . To support interprofessional practice, health providers should: • create a safe environment where differing opinions are welcome • validate and acknowledge differing perspectives • communicate positively and constructively • see conflict with the potential for a positive outcome 5. Teamwork: A multidisciplinary team is a group of individuals from different professional backgrounds, each bringing their own specialized expertise to work together on a common goal which is achieving patient-centered care. 6. Transparency of duties and responsibilities: This competence helps all team members to understand their own and others' roles and duties and use one another's knowledge and skills to perform the right task. Significance of Inter/Intra professional relation in healthcare settings: Both are increasingly recognized as important due to the complex and dynamic nature of healthcare organizations and the growing specialization of healthcare professions. They are essential to: 1. Enhances patient care and outcomes When healthcare professionals work together, they can provide comprehensive and well-coordinated care by ensuring that all aspects of a patient’s condition are addressed, leading to more accurate diagnoses and treatment plans. 2. Mitigates medical errors According to the Joint Commission, miscommunication during patient handoffs contributes to an estimated 80% of serious medical errors. By working together, 5 healthcare providers can identify and address potential safety issues more effectively regarding medication management, patient handoffs, and care transitions, which are critical points for errors. 3. Expedites initiation of treatment A substantial proportion of healthcare is marked by waiting periods. Patients await physician consultations and physicians await input from other interprofessional team members. Communication delays allow medical conditions to deteriorate. A clinical collaboration platform efficiently delivers pertinent information to the right individuals at the right time via secure messaging, voice, or video leading to a better quality of care. 4. Diminishes inefficiencies and healthcare costs Interprofessional collaboration ensures more efficient resource utilization, leading to cost savings and improved resource allocation. For example, when a team of professionals collaborates on a patient’s care plan, unnecessary tests and procedures and duplicated work can be avoided, reducing both the financial burden on patients and the strain on healthcare facilities. 5. Advances staff relations and job satisfaction Optimizing clinical workflows through improved interdisciplinary collaboration helps reduce burnout and improve clinician satisfaction. On the contrary, poor intra- and interprofessional teamwork is associated with higher rates of inadequate or missed care, medical errors

Physicians' primary ethical obligation to individual patients is to diagnose and treat illnesses through using their expertise, ensure patients receive the best possible care plus educate patients about their conditions and treatments to make informed decisions about their health. A physician who suspects that an adverse reaction to a drug or medical device has occurred, whatever its severity, has an ethical responsibility to manage these adverse events and to communicate that information to the professional community through established reporting mechanisms. Physicians involved in the media environment should be aware of their ethical obligations to patients, the public, and the medical profession; and that their conduct can affect their medical colleagues, other health care professionals, as well as institutions with which they are affiliated. Media includes both the traditional media (radio and TV) and the new social media platforms. E-Professionalism is the professional use of electronic platforms. It includes online attitudes, actions, and adherence to relevant professional codes of conduct and principles including honesty, integrity, reliability, responsibility, and respect. 6. E-professionalism and ethical conduct in the media: 6. E-professionalism and ethical conduct in the media: Physicians should: Always remember that they are physicians first and foremost, and must uphold the values, norms, and integrity of the medical profession. Know that sharing information would threaten public health due to the spread of false perceptions and opinions. Reveal their identity (name and qualification) when sharing medical content. It is not acceptable to make an anonymous profile and share medical content with the public through it. You are completely responsible for your shared content. Never to disclose patient’s information on media. 6. E-professionalism and ethical conduct in the media: Aware that any information they share on media, may be disseminated to a larger audience and are difficult to remove as other users may distribute it further or comment on it. So, the shared information should be: Truthful and accurate. Concise. Up to date. Easy for patients to understand. Clear from any uncertain content that could be taken out of the situation. Physicians at all stages of their professional lives need to be able to recognize when they are and when they are not able to provide appropriate care for patients. CME about recent medical technology and advancements. Cultivate continuous self-awareness and self-observation. Seek feedback from peers and others. Maintain their own health and wellness. Be attentive to environmental and other factors that may compromise their ability to bring appropriate skills to the care of individual patients and act in the patient’s best interest. props.text: CONSENT BY PROF. DR. SOMAYA MADKOUR Forensic Medicine and Clinical Toxicology ILO’s. To apply knowledge of the ethical imperative for informed consent in the doctor-patient relationship (and its limits) Differentiate types of consents in the medical field. Apply the principals of informed consent and how to be valid and documented. Differentiate the exceptions to require a consent. Respect the patient’s right to refuse treatment. It lies at the heart of the relationship between the patient and the health care professional. The patient relies on the professional’s expertise, knowledge and advice, but it is up to the patient to decide whether he/she will accept or reject treatment, or in some circumstances request that the professional make the decision Consent is a central topic in bioethics. What does consent mean?? Consent is the giving of permission or agreement for an intervention (whether diagnostic or therapeutic) following a process of communication about the proposed intervention. Consent must be obtained before starting treatment or investigations, or providing personal or social care for a patient or involving a patient in teaching and research. All patients have the right to be involved in decisions about their treatment and care and to make informed decisions if they can. The exchange of information between doctor and patient is essential to good decision making. serious harm can result if patients are not listened to, or if they are not given the information they need - and time and support to understand it - so they can make informed decisions about their care. Obtaining valid consent is an ethical obligation and legal compulsion Informed consent is essential to ethics, which upholds the principles of autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. Treating a patient without informed consent could result in legal action for assault against the Health Practitioner who provided the care, irrespective of whether the patient suffered harm as a result of the procedure (constitutes medical malpractice). Consent in medical practice is needed in the following situations: 1-Examination of a patient for the purpose of diagnosis and subsequent treatment. 2- Examination of a patient for medico-legal purposes. 3- Involving patients in medical research studies. Why is consent important? To protect the patient from unauthorized procedures. To protect the physician from claims of malpractice. If the consent is not obtained, the patient has the right to sue for medical malpractice Implied consent (Known by the behavior of the patient) The act of a patient entering a doctor's chamber and expressing his problem is taken as an implied consent for general physical examination (patient has consented to abdominal palpation when voluntarily undressing and lying on couch) and routine investigations such as X-rays etc… When he/she offers an arm for venipuncture (giving a blood sample). The act of the patient standing in line to receive a vaccination. 2- Express (oral or written) consent It means that the Patient expressly asks the doctor to provide care and consents by direct words, oral or written. This consent should be obtained for any procedure that carries any risk, and therefore, patient-specific agreement must be obtained before the procedure starts. The patient or his/her representative has the right to be provided with sufficient information by the physician to allow him/her to make an informed decision to decide whether or not to consent to a certain procedure. Types of consent Oral consent is valid, but it is usual to obtain written consent for major procedures. Oral consent: For intimate examinations e.g., vaginal and rectal. Simple procedures e.g., insertion of an intravenous cannula. Procedures performed under local anesthesia e.g., suture of minor lacerations. Written consent: For more invasive tests or for major procedures with significant risks e.g. blood transfusion breast biopsy all operations requiring general or spinal anesthesia. WHAT ARE THE REQUIREMENTS FOR OBTAINING A VALID CONSENT? the patient giving consent must have capacity the consent must be freely given the consent must be sufficiently specific to the procedure or treatment proposed the consent must be informed. 9 Capacity The patient must have the capacity to give consent. A person has decision making capacity if they can: understand the facts and choices involved weigh up the consequences and evaluate the personal cost and benefit of each of the consequences and relate them to your own set of values and priorities communicate their decision. Legally, adults are presumed to have capacity to consent to or refuse medical treatment unless otherwise indicated. A person is incapable of giving consent to the carrying out of medical treatment if the person: (a) is incapable of understanding the general nature and effect of the proposed treatment, or (b) is incapable of indicating whether or not he or she consents or does not consent to the treatment being carried out General principles to follow when assessing capacity Always presume a person has capacity Capacity is decision-specific (for example capacity may fluctuate or certain simple health treatments may be within a person’s capacity to consent whilst others may not) Respect a person’s privacy Substitute decision making is a last resort Freely given Consent must be freely given. The patient must not be pressured, coerced or intimidated into giving consent by Health Service staff, a Health Practitioner, a carer or a family member. Sufficiently specific The consent must be specific and is valid only for the condition being treated and the specified treatment or procedure about which the patient has been informed and agreed to. Informed The patient must be informed in broad terms of the nature and purpose in a way that the patient can understand. Health Practitioners have a duty to provide the patient with enough information to enable them to gain an understanding of the nature and effects of the operation, procedure or treatment, the risks associated with it and any alternatives to the proposed treatment. This obligation includes the use of different communication tools as necessary, including shared decision making So consent must be given voluntary by an appropriately informed patient who has the capacity to consent to the proposed procedure . If the patient does not know what the intervention entails …. it is not consent If patients are not able to do all of the components, family members, court-appointed guardians, or others (as determined by law) may act as "surrogate decision-makers" and make decisions for you. A valid Consent is not given for illegal act as criminal abortion and euthanasia. Sometimes ethical beliefs and legal rights do not always coincide. We cannot legally consent to voluntary euthanasia, since it is illegal, even if we feel strongly that it should be permitted. A valid Informed Consent should be obtained by a health care provider who is involved with the patient's care The seven principles of decision making and consent Doctors must start from the presumption that all adult patients have capacity to make decisions about their treatment and care. A patient can only be judged to lack capacity to make a specific decision at a specific time, and only after assessment in line with legal requirements The choice of treatment or care for patients who lack capacity must be of overall benefit to them, and decisions should be made in consultation with those who are close to them or advocating for them Patients whose right to consent is affected by law should be supported to be involved in the decision-making process, and to exercise choice if possible All patients have the right to be involved in decisions about their treatment and care and be supported to make informed decisions if they are able. Decision making is an ongoing process focused on meaningful dialogue All patients have the right to be listened to, and to be given the information they need to make a decision and the time and support they need to understand it. Doctors must try to find out what matters to patients so they can share relevant information about the benefits and harms of proposed options and reasonable alternatives, including the option to take no action. Shared decision making The exchange of information between doctor and patient is central to good decision making. Discuss with the patients diagnosis and prognosis uncertainties about the diagnosis or prognosis, including options for further investigations options for treating or managing the condition, including the option to take no action the nature of each option, what would be involved, and the desired outcome You must give patients clear, accurate and up-to-date information, based on the best available evidence, about the potential benefits and risks of harm of each option, including the option to take no action. (By ‘harm’ we mean any potential negative outcome, including a side effect or complication) To help patients understand and retain relevant information you should: share it in a place and at a time when they are most likely to understand and retain it specially distressing and, if so, be considerate when sharing it accommodate a patient’s wishes if they would like anyone else or a relative, partner, friend, or advocate – to be involved in discussions ( especially when breaking bad news ) and/or help them make decisions give them time and opportunity to consider it before and after making a decision specially with information that is complex or involving significant risk Also make sure that the patient knows if there is time limits to make their own decision and who they can contact in health care team if they have any question Finally respect their decision even the patient refuses (option to take no action) you should sensitively encourage them to think about what they might want to happen if they become unable to make healthcare decisions. Such discussions might include: the patient’s wishes and fears, their preferences about future options for care, and the values and priorities that influence their decision making any treatment or care the patient might want to refuse, and in what circumstances any interventions that might become necessary in an emergency, such as cardiopulmonary resuscitation whether the patient would like anyone else – relatives, friends, carers or representatives – to be involved in decisions about their care If a patient has a condition that is likely to impair their capacity as it progresses, 17 Exceptions to requirement of consent Mentally incapacitated patient: Minor (child): less than 18 years Comatose patient: In emergency requiring immediate action, only to save the patient’s life or avoid major deterioration of the patient's health. Third-party consent; The patient is mentally incapable of understanding the procedure and/or the ramifications of consent or refusal, so consent is given or withheld on their behalf by a legal designate, eg a parent or guardian in the case of children, or a power of attorney delegated by a person suffering a degenerative neural disease. 5-Certain occupations involving public risk: e.g. food dealers and drivers cannot refuse to have checkup tests. 6- Imprisoned patient: The legal authority can give consent for him. 18 How should consent be documented? It is essential to document clearly the person’s agreement to the intervention and the discussions that led up to that agreement particularly if: The intervention is invasive, complex or involves significant risks; There may be significant consequences for employment, or social or personal life. Agreement can be documented by a signature (or mark if unable to write) on a consent form or through documenting in their notes that they have given verbal consent. Documentation should be dated and signed by the patient or guardian. should be prepared in duplicate and a copy given to the patient. The original form should be kept, like all other medical records, as a legal document that the patient agreed to the treatment. Informed Consent, The Right to Refuse Treatment patients who are legally competent have have the legal and moral right to refuse any or all treatment. This is true even if the patient chooses to make a "bad decision" that may result in serious disability or even death. Like consent to medical treatment, a refusal of treatment must be: • freely given • specific; and • informed. The patient should be asked to sign an Against Medical Advice (AMA) form to protect the health care provider from legal liability for not providing the disputed treatment. Refusing a test, treatment, or procedure does not necessarily mean that you are refusing all care. The next best treatment should always be offered to anyone who refuses the recommended care. 20 The reasons may include: Religious beliefs Cultural beliefs Worrying about risks and chances of success of a certain procedure. Thank you!

props.text: 1 Dr/ Somaya Madkour Professor of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology Alexandria University 2 Confidentiality ILO’s. 1- Define medical confidentiality& its importance in the medical field. 2. Contrast how and when breach of confidentiality take place. 3. Apply the principles that should be followed on allowing breach of Confidentiality Confidentiality Confidentiality is one of the core duties of medical practice. It requires health care providers to keep a patient’s personal health information private unless consent to release the information is provided by the patient Medical Secret: is defined as “Any medical information that comes to the knowledge of the practitioners as a result of their work whether directly obtained from the patient, or otherwise” • It includes any information that the doctor knows about the patient (alive or dead), that a patient may deem its disclosure undesirable or harmful to his health, reputation, financial, social or professional status. • It includes any information about the patient’s identity, condition, diagnosis, investigations’ results, treatment, and/or prognosis (whether chances of cure, disability, or death Confidentiality covers also communications between the patient and the doctor. Generally, this also includes communications between the patient and other professional staff working with the doctor. - Respect for confidentiality is firmly established in codes of medical ethics. Hippocratic Oath "What I may see or hear in the course of the treatment or even outside of the treatment in regard to the life of men, which on no account one must spread abroad, I will keep to myself, holding such things shameful to be spoken about". Ethical considerations Confidentiality can be considered from a number of different ethical perspectives • Respect for patient autonomy Any breach of confidentiality means that the patient’s autonomy has not been respected, whether or not the patient is aware of the breach. • Implied promise 3 The physician -patient relationship could be seen as having elements of an implied contract and this could include an implied promise that health professionals keep information about their patients confidential. If confidentiality is subsequently breached the patient may feel that a promise has been broken. • Consequentialism The question of whether it is wrong to breach confidentiality is determined by the consequences of the breach. Breach of confidentiality could result in loss of trust in the physician, and perhaps doctors generally, resulting in him not accessing healthcare in the future with a bad effect on his (and others?) health. On the other hand, there may be situations where there are bad consequences of not breaching confidentiality (sexually transmitted diseases). Why is confidentiality important? a) It creates a trusting environment that allow patients to openly and confidently share complete health information, resulting in a stronger physician-patient relationship and better delivery of care. b) It may also increase the patient’s willingness to seek care. For conditions that might be stigmatizing, such as reproductive, sexual, public health, and psychiatric health concerns, confidentiality assures that private information will not be disclosed to family or employers without their consent. c) Legal disciplinary action: Data breaches can result in everything from fines to prison sentences for those responsible. The Principles of Confidentiality • The obligation of confidentiality prohibits the health care provider from disclosing information about the patient's case to others without permission and encourages the providers and health care systems to take precautions to ensure that only authorized access occurs. • If the patients’ conditions require that information about them be discussed among members of a health care team; all team members have authorized access to confidential information about the patients and have a duty of protecting such information. • Patient confidentiality is protected under the law. If a patient's private information is disclosed without authorization and causes some type of harm to the patient, he could have a cause of action against the medical provider or malpractice. How Long Does Doctor-Patient Confidentiality Last? 4 The duty of confidentiality continues even after a patient has stopped seeing or being treated by that particular doctor. The duty even survives the death of a patient. When can confidentiality be breached? However, medical confidentiality is not absolute in modern medicine. There are occasions when there is a need to breach this idealism. The three general principles underlying disclosures are: a) Disclosures with permission of the patient b) Disclosures required by law; c) Disclosures in the public interest A) Disclosures with permission of the patient: The patient has given express consent (oral or written) to disclosure. Other disclosures may be justified on the presumption of implied consent for example, a sedated patient on intensive care unit (ICU). Any decision made on behalf of an individual lacking capacity to disclose should be done so proportionately and in their best interests. Also, disclosures of personal information take place between members of a healthcare team. Disclosures should always be limited to reveal only the relevant and appropriate information. Disclosure to relatives (only for the patient’s best interests) when they must care for the patient at home, except when the patient refuses. If the patient is incompetent or minor, it is obvious that all possible information should be given to the parents or guardians. Also for the sake of the patient , In emergencies , you should pass relevant information promptly to those providing the patient’s care. B) Disclosures required by law; 1- : Road Traffic accident All citizens, including doctors, must provide the police, on request, with information (name, address), which might identify a driver alleged to have committed a traffic offence. A doctor may have a legal obligation to inform the responsible authority if he has concerns that a patient has a medical disability that could affect his driving. 2- Prevention or detection of crime: To safe guard national security (Prevention of Terrorism): All citizens, including doctors, must inform police, as soon as possible, of any information that may help to prevent an act of terrorism, or help in apprehending or prosecuting a terrorist 3- Legal requirements: notification of births, deaths, stillbirths, therapeutic abortions, drug addiction. 5 The doctor has a duty to notify a birth. Stillbirths (a baby born dead after 24th week of pregnancy) must be registered. Doctors attending patients during their last illness must sign a death certificate, giving the cause of death. 4- Other exceptions under legal basis: (in case of malpractice suits). To defend a charge against a healthcare practitioner alleged by the patient or his/her family. Disclosure should be only to the official authorities C) Disclosures for Public safety: 1: Concern for the safety of other specific persons The criminal procedure law (قانون الإجراءات الجنائية) states that every person that knows about a crime should notify it. Obviously, when it comes to the knowledge of a doctor that a crime is about to be committed, whether the information comes to him in the course of his professional work or not, it is his duty as a citizen to prevent it. 2: Legal requirements to report certain communicable or infectious diseases to the health authorities. The law requires the report of certain communicable/infectious diseases to the public health authorities. In these cases, the duty to protect public health outweighs the duty to maintain a patient's confidence as in cases of sexually transmitted diseases. D) Disclosures for other purposes: 1- For life insurance companies: a physician should examine a person before he gets a life insurance. He should be honest when informing the insurance company about his medical condition. In cases where previous knowledge of some disease has been acquired by the medical officer, and at the time of examination no sign of it is present, he cannot legally report it, for the report would be a breach of confidence and actionable. 2- To comply with mandatory reporting duties (Victims of neglect or abuse for any person): when there is suspicion of child abuse. Abuse or neglect of the elderly is also required to be reported. Also Other vulnerable persons abuse (Abuse of Disabled Persons) should be reported. Principles that should be followed on allowing breach of confidentiality • It must be to proper authorities. • Not beyond what is required or relevant or keep disclosures to the minimum necessary for the purpose • Reason for disclosure must be documented in the medical records. You must document in the patient’s record your reasons for disclosing information with or without consent. You must also document any 6 steps you have taken to seek the patient’s consent, to inform them about the disclosure, or your reasons for not doing so. • On accusing a physician of divulging patient’s secret There are three points that should be considered in accusing a physician of divulging patient’s secret: 1. There was divulging of a secret. 2.The secret was known to the physician through his profession. 3. The disclosure of the secret lead to harm or damage to the patient (physical or psychological). • To safeguard the protection of patient confidentiality, it is important to adhere to the following recommended practices: 1. Make sure doors and partitions are closed when discussing confidential information, particularly in locations like the emergency department where privacy is difficult to ensure. 2. Avoid discussing patient information within earshot of unauthorized persons. 3. Limit health information conveyed and number of colleagues, consultants, or other staff receiving the patient’s information to what is necessary for the identification, evaluation, and treatment of patients. 4. Maintain privacy of paper and electronic medical records and electronic communication, such as by locking computers when stepping away and only using encrypted email to discuss patients. 5. Do not share passwords that may lead to the compromise of and unauthorized access to computerized patient information. 7. Obtain informed consent before disclosing information to third parties (family, friends, law enforcement officers, observers such as students) or allowing them to visit. 8. Obtain written informed consent before recording or filming the patient and before disseminating, publishing, or broadcasting patient images or information. Further reading General Medical Council. Confidentiality: Good practice in handling patient information. Manchester: General Medical Council; 2017. Department of Health. Confidentiality: NHS Code of Practice 2010 . Supplementary Guidance: Public Interest Disclosures (November ) http://www.dh.gov.uk/prod_consum_dh/groups/dh_digitalassets/@dh/ 7 @en/@ps/documents/digitalasset/dh_122031.pdf accessed 21 January 2013)

props.text: HUMAN RIGHTS BY PROF. DR. SOMAYA MADKOUR Forensic Medicine and Clinical Toxicology ILO’s Define human rights Characteristics of Human Rights Appreciate the Importance of human rights Recognize basic human rights Codes of Hammurabi Magna Carta (1215) Holocaust Nazi Human Experiments Mass killings Torture Forced displacement of millions of civilians Attacks on civilians in cities through widespread bombing The atrocities of World War II created a global consensus that human rights were a universal concern that required international action. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) Foundation of modern human rights Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948 This was the first comprehensive international agreement on human rights, establishing a "common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations” Human rights are the basic rights and freedom that belong to all people in the world, from birth to death. These rights are based on shared values like: Dignity Equality Fairness Respect Independence HUMAN RIGHTS These ethics are protected and defined by the laws of various countries. Human rights law: obliges governments to do some things, and prevents them from doing others. Individuals also have responsibilities: in using their human rights, they must respect the rights of others. No government, group or individual person has the right to do anything that violates another’s rights. CHARACTERISTICS OF HUMAN RIGHTS Human rights are universal and inalienable. As all people are born with the same rights even, they live anywhere. These rights are inalienable, which cannot be taken away, or no one has to deprive them without any reason. Universality and inalienability (not subject to being taken away from or absolute) العالمية وعدم قابلية التصرف (لا تخضع للانتزاع أو التنازل المطلق) Human rights are indivisible. It can’t be divisible to rich and poor, caste, religion, sex, and others; all rights have equal status for everyone. Whether civil, political, economic, social or cultural in nature, they are all inherent to the dignity of every human person. These rights cannot be positioned in any order in any condition. So, in this way, human rights are indivisible. 2. Indivisibility: عدم قابلية التجزئة For example, the realization of the right to health may depend on the realization of the right to education or of the right to information. 3. Inter-dependence and inter-relatedness الترابط All individuals are equal as human beings. No discrimination of any kind, such as race, color, sex, ethnicity, age, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, disability, property, birth or other status. 4. Equality and non-discrimination: المساواة وعدم التمييز 5. Legally protected Rights are necessary: As in the absence of rights, physical and social welfare is impossible, as it also provides various conditions that help to uplift the people. So human rights are vital and essential to have. 1) Human rights ensure people have basic needs met For everyone, there are requirements for food, cloth, shelter, and medicine. These are the basics necessities that are crucial for every human life. By including these in a person’s basic human rights, everyone has a baseline level of dignity. 2) Human rights protect vulnerable groups from abuse The Significance of Human Rights 3) Human rights give people access to education Education is one of the top priorities which are essential for society. Without education, poverty is ordinary. It is based on schooling, supplies, private schools, or government schools. As education is for everyone, the people have an equal right to this. Seeing education as a right means everyone can get access, not just the elite. The Significance of Human Rights 4) Human rights encourage equal work opportunities The concept of human rights provides a guide for how workers should be treated and encourages equality. The Significance of Human Rights 5) Human rights allow people to stand up to societal corruption The concept of human rights allows people to speak up when they experience abuse and corruption. This is why specific rights like the right to assemble are so crucial because no society is perfect. The concept of human rights empowers people and tells them that they deserve dignity from society. When they don’t receive it, they can stand up. The Significance of Human Rights 6) Human rights provide a universal standard that holds governments accountable With a standard for what is a human right, governments can be held accountable for their actions. The Significance of Human Rights 7) Human rights protect the environment We live in the world, we need the land, so it makes sense that what happens to the environment impacts humanity. The right to clean air, clean soil, and clean water are all as important as the other rights included in this list. The Significance of Human Rights Why Human Rights Matter in Healthcare Why medical students should study human rights? Foundation of Medical Ethics: Human rights principles—such as dignity, equality, and autonomy—form the basis of medical ethics. Respect for Patient Autonomy: respect informed consent, confidentiality, and the right to make personal health decisions. Protection of Vulnerable Groups: such as refugees, prisoners, or those with mental illness. Preventing Participation in Abuses: (e.g., unethical experiments or torture). Professional Responsibility: to report any act of human rights abuse. Global Health and Social Justice: Health is recognized as a human right. Understanding this helps doctors advocate for fair access to healthcare. Legal and Institutional Awareness of international standards and national laws. Categories of Human Rights These are the privileges an individual has as a member of a community and are guaranteed by the Law for him to engage in all forms of political activities in the community they include the right to vote, to freedom of speech and to obtain information. These are the rights every individual has to engage in without fear, or favor to perform one’s duty and obligations as a citizen. (e.g.. right to a name, right to freedom from discrimination, right to equality before the law, right to public trial, right to marry, right to leave a country, etc.). These rights allow people to live in conditions that promote well-being (right to education, health care, food, clothing, shelter and social security) and to interact with people and participate in society without violating laws (e.g.. freedom of conscience, thought and freedom of association). These allows individuals to preserve their customs and traditions and as well practice their unique way of life (e.g.. the right to freedom of religion, and to speak the language, and to practice the culture of one’s choice) Ensures every person has access to the basic economic resources and opportunities to live with dignity and security e.g. wages, working hours, welfare. This declaration consists of 30 articles affirming an individual’s rights. Those 30 articles currently known as 30 universal declaration of human rights or 30 basic human rights Universal Declaration of Human Rights United Nations General Assembly 10 December 1948 Article 1 Free and equal All human beings are born free and equal and should be treated the same way. Article 2 Freedom from discrimination Everyone can claim their rights regardless of sex, race, language, religion, social standing, etc. Article 3 Right to life Everyone has the right to life and to live in freedom and safety. Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person. Article 4 Freedom from slavery No one has the right to treat you as a slave nor should you enslave anyone. Article 5 Freedom from torture No one has the right to torture you. Article 6 Right to recognition before the law You should be legally protected in the same way everywhere like anyone else. Article 7 Right to equality before the law The law is the same for everyone and should be applied in the same manner to all. All are equal before the law and are entitled to equal protection of the law. Article 8 Access to justice You have the right to obtain legal help and access the justice system when your rights are not respected. Article 9 Freedom from arbitrary detention No one can arrest or detain you arbitrarily , or send you away from your country unjustly. Article 10 Right to a fair trial Trials should be public and tried in a fair manner by an impartial and independent tribunal. Article 11 Presumption of innocence You are considered innocent until it can be proved you are guilty according to law. If accused of a crime you have the right to a defense. Article 12 Right to privacy You have the right to protection if someone tried to harm your good name, enter your home without permission or interfere with your correspondence. Article 13 Freedom of movement You have the right to leave or move within your own country and you should be able to return. Article 14 Right to asylum If you are persecuted at home, you have the right to seek protection in another country. Article 15 Right to nationality You have the right to belong to a country and have a nationality. Article 16 Right to marriage and to found a family Men and women have the right to marry when they are legally able without limits due to race, nationality or religion. Families should be protected by the Government and the justice system. Article 18 Freedom of religion or belief Everyone has the right to freely manifest their religion, to change it and to practice it alone or with others. Article 17 Right to own property You have the right to own things. No one has the right to illegally take them from you. Article 20 Freedom of assembly You have the right to organize and participate in peaceful meetings. Article 19 Freedom of Expression Everyone has the right to think and say what they like and no one should forbid it. Article 21 Right to partake in public affairs Everyone has the right to take part in their country’s political affairs and equal access to public service. Governments should be voted for regularly. Article 22 Right to social security Society should help individuals to freely develop and make the most of all advantages offered in their country. Article 23 Right to work Everyone has the right to work in favorable conditions and be free to choose your work with a salary that allows you to live and support family. Everyone should receive equal pay for equal work. Article 24 Right to leisure and rest Each work day should not be too long and everyone has the right to rest and take regular paid holidays. Article 27 Right to take part in cultural, artistic and scientific life You have the right to share the benefits of your community’s culture, arts and sciences. Article 26 Right to education You have the right to go to school, continue your studies as far as you wish and learn regardless of race, religion or country of origin. Article 25 Right to adequate standard of living You have the right to have what you need so that you and your family do not go hungry, homeless or fall ill. Article 29 Duty to your community You have duties toward the community within which your personality can fully develop. The law should guarantee human rights. It should allow everyone to respect others and to be respected. Article 30 Rights are inalienable No one, institution nor individual, should act in any way to destroy the rights enshrined in the UDHR. Article 28 Right to a free and fair world To make sure your rights are respected, there must be an order that can protect them. This order should be global. The UDHR was developed mainly in response to: Economic crisis World War II atrocities Industrial Revolution Globalization B A government bans physicians from joining medical associations. This violates which human right? Freedom of assembly and association Right to nationality Right to seek asylum Right to education A woman is denied the right to make medical decisions for herself because of her gender. Which UDHR principle is most directly breached? A. Freedom of movement B. Equality and freedom from discrimination C. Right to property D. Right to political participation B A 60-year-old man with advanced heart disease refuses surgery after being fully informed of the risks and benefits. The medical team honors his decision and provides supportive care instead. This situation reflects the patient’s human right to: Freedom of expression Informed consent and autonomy in medical decisions Equal access to healthcare Confidentiality of medical records B A physician refuses to treat a refugee because they lack official identification. This action violates which UDHR principle? Right to nationality Right to recognition before the law Right to equal access to healthcare and non-discrimination Right to seek asylum C Thank You

props.text: the College of nurses of Ontario presents confidentiality and privacy case studies this presentation is the second of two webcast chapters about privacy and confidentiality the first chapter was an overview of your obligations and accountabilities related to maintaining the privacy and confidentiality of clients personal health information in this chapter we will review some case studies and reflect on how to apply the concepts we learned in the first chapter to situations that could result in privacy breaches after listening to this webcast you should be able to reflect on your practice in relation to confidentiality and privacy apply the principles of confidentiality and privacy to your practice apply the elements of care to your practice as identified in chapter 1 privacy breaches are serious offenses that negatively affect the trust between nurses and their clients to maintain this trust nurses need to keep their clients as the focus of Care by always applying the three elements of care professionalism ethics and therapeutic relationships when you apply these three elements you make the client the center of your nursing care as you review the case studies in this webcast consider how the absence of these three elements when dealing with clients health information can lead to privacy breaches and erosion of trust let's review the first case study a nurse posted the following comment on her social media page can this shift be any longer it started out with a waiting room full of nagging people that don't seem to know what emergency means then I had to deal with the trauma of trying to transfer a 400 pound no joke intubated COPD patient down the hall to the ICU those ICU nurses are such divas and I wasn't in the mood for their whining anyone around ABC Hospital want to save me with a drink to get me through the next 10 hours of my shift if you read this post would you be able to identify the client while you may have a privacy setting on your account this does not guarantee that other people will not see your post when posting information on social media sites such as Facebook ask yourself whether the information you are sharing could possibly reveal the identity of the client even if you didn't include any names reflect on the possible outcomes of posting inappropriate content on social media anything that exists on the Internet is there forever and could be retrieved even after you have deleted it you must protect any information you learn about clients in your care clients need to be confident that their nurse will protect their personal information and basic dignity as discussed in the previous slide about elements of care if you breach this trust even unintentionally it can damage the nurse-client relationship co-worker relationships and the general trustworthiness of the nursing profession case 2 use of pictures a nurse educator from a tropical Disease Clinic is preparing a presentation poster for an infectious diseases conference she includes pictures of varying stages of a client's lesions in this poster in this scenario what factors does this nurse need to consider although the client is not directly identified in this scenario pictures can provide information that makes it possible to identify the client in addition the conference attendees in this scenario are not in this client Circle of Care therefore they should not be receiving this information about the client according to the college's consent practice guideline nurses are accountable for obtaining consent you must consider whether the client has given you consent to share the photo also organizations often have policies about taking and sharing photos of clients if the client has consented make sure you document this consent to learn more about consent and The Circle of Care view chapter 1 of this webcast titled confidentiality and privacy an overview case 3 sharing information Marcus was admitted to the hospital from the long-term care facility he was diagnosed with dehydration and delirium he is expected to eventually return to the facility the charge nurse at the facility calls for an update of Marcus's status can the hospital nurse share this information with a long-term care facility in the scenario both the long-term care facility and the hospital are considered health information custodians as we discussed in chapter one of this webcast titled confidentiality in privacy and overview health information custodians or their agents can assume they have a client's implied consent to share their personal health information the nurse at the hospital can give the long-term care facility updates on Marcus's status because the purpose would be to assist in providing Health Care to Marcus an exception would be if the hospital nurse is aware that Marcus or his substitute decision maker has specifically requested not to share that information with the long-term care facility case 4 Family Ties Adam works on the Cardiology unit at the hospital and learns that his grandfather was admitted overnight he has not been able to get in touch with his grandfather while on the computer getting results for his client Adam checks his grandfather's health record to find out what room he is in and why he has been admitted is it acceptable for Adam to access his grandfather's health record in this scenario Adam is not in The Circle of Care for his grandfather because he is neither providing Health Care nor assisting in providing Health Care to his grandfather this case demonstrates how health care workers can easily cross the line and breach an individual's right to privacy and confidentiality before accessing a client's health record ask yourself do I need to know this information to provide health care or assist in providing Health Care to this individual being an employee of a health facility and even signing a confidentiality agreement upon employment does not give you permission to look up information that is beyond what you need to provide Health Care to a client regardless of whether the client is your family member case 5 communicating through technology Dr Skinner orders a blood test for your patient she asks you to text the results to her so she can text back a medication order you need to use your own personal phone to text The Physician what should you consider to maintain privacy and confidentiality using technology to communicate a test result or accept an order does not change the standard for protecting clients information you must consider how the use of Technology may affect the security of the information that is being transmitted and ensure measures are in place to protect the information such as encryption or the use of passwords read the college's documentation practice standard to learn more about ensuring the security of information when using personal devices k-6 client from previous shift you work part-time for a community Agency on your last shift you took care of David an older gentleman with renal failure who lives alone on your next shift you decide to check David's chart to see how he is doing are you still in David's Circle of Care unless you are still providing or assisting in providing Health Care to David you are no longer in his Circle of Care as we discussed in chapter 1 of this webcast titled confidentiality and privacy and overview if you are not in a client's Circle of Care then you do not have implied consent to access the client's health record curiosity or concern are not professional reasons to access health information even if it is for a former client being a nurse puts you in a position to access clients personal health information but you are accountable for knowing when to use or refrain from using that access the six case studies we reviewed in this chapter show the importance of applying the college's practice documents and Concepts such as consent and the elements of care to situations involving personal health information this will help you maintain the confidentiality of clients health information and only share necessary information within the Circle of Care remember privacy breaches erode the trust between nurses and clients and affect the Public's trust in the nursing profession therefore protecting the confidentiality and privacy of personal health information is essential for providing clients with the best care possible if you have questions about this webcast or about confidentiality and privacy in general please contact the college
